paragraphs: Welcome to Hebleo, the smart way to learn Hebrew. I’ve spent over ten years bringing together three kinds of experience:
numberedList: Learning languages independently and seeing what works first-hand.
Teaching Hebrew and refining my materials with each student.
My M.Sc. in Cognitive Science, which helped me understand how to improve learning, especially languages.

paragraphs: One of my students, Adam, started with no Hebrew and a similar scientific background. We tested how long it would take him to hold conversations with me in Hebrew.
For an English speaker, this usually takes around 500 hours. Using the method at the core of Hebleo, Adam took around 70 hours—over seven times faster.
Let’s try a short demonstration. These ideas can help you learn beyond this course, too.

pages.title: A quick memory experiment

paragraphs: Press Play to see a number for ten seconds. Remember as much as you can without writing it down. When it disappears, type what you remember.

pages.prompt: What do you remember? Enter an attempt, or select Show me how.

feedback.partial: That was a lot of digits to hold in mind! Let me show you a way to make sense of them.
feedback.exact: You remembered it. Now let me show you a way to organise the same information.

paragraphs: Let’s give the same digits some meaning.

descriptions: The same digits, grouped into two sets of eight.

principles.title: Chunking:
principles.text: Think of two meaningful dates instead of sixteen separate digits.

principles.title: Logical constraints:
principles.text: A date limits the possibilities: months run from 01 to 12, and a day cannot be 47.

principles.title: Memory hooks:
principles.text: Connect new information to established old knowledge. If you know these events and their dates, they give the digits something familiar to connect to. If not, grouping and date structure can still help.

events: July 4, 1776 — the American Declaration of Independence.
dateContext.transition: Same digits, different meaning. Three ideas help:

paragraphs: We’ll use all three principles, starting with memory hooks: connecting new information to established old knowledge. First, we’ll build on things you know from English. Later, we’ll connect new Hebrew concepts to Hebrew you’ve already learned.

inlineOptional.label: Try the comparison (optional)

paragraphs: Think of the two dates and type what you remember, without looking back. Then compare your attempts and notice what helped.

inlineOptional.prompt: With the two dates in mind, what do you remember?

feedback.exact: That’s the original sequence. Notice which part of the connection helped you bring it back.
feedback.reverse: You recalled both dates, but swapped their order. The original starts with July 4, 1776, then September 11, 2001.
feedback.zeros: You recalled the dates. In the original display, months and days use two digits: 07/04 and 09/11. Those zeroes are part of the original sequence.
feedback.dayMonth: You used day–month–year. These are the same dates; the demonstration uses month–day–year, so its sequence begins 07/04/1776.
feedback.partial: Here’s the original number alongside your attempt. Compare the two date groups and notice which parts came back to you.
feedback.empty: Here are the two dates within the original number. Notice how the grouping, format and familiar events can help you make sense of it.

paragraphs: Next, we’ll use familiar concepts from English to learn your first four Hebrew letters. See you in the next lesson!
